utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all. We are supposed to hear the evidence of General Rose today, and I was informed that there's something for you, Mr. Robinson, to raise before we hear the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I had notified the Chamber and the Prosecution, by e-mail last week, that we would be objecting to certain paragraphs of the amalgamated statement when offered as evidence under Rule 92 ter. And the particular paragraphs relate to the fighting in Gorazde in April and May of 1994, which are paragraphs 66 through 113 of the amalgamated statement; the fighting in Bihac in November of 19 November, which is paragraphs, I believe, 169 through 176 of the amalgamated statement; and one additional matter which I hadn't raised in my e-mail is that we object to paragraphs 218 and 219 at the very end, which we think are conclusory statements that would not otherwise be admissible if offered as part of live testimony, and we think they should be excluded from the statement. The basis of our objection is twofold; first, notice, and, second, relevance. With respect to notice, I would point out that neither the Gorazde nor Bihac events are charged in the indictment, and they don't appear in any of the schedules of killings in detention camps, or otherwise, or acts of persecution, shellings or snipings. We did receive a pre-trial brief in which, in paragraph 53, there is a reference to Gorazde and Bihac, where it indicates that meanwhile the VRS continued military actions in a manner which demonstrates a connection between the strategic objectives and military operations, including the 1993 through 1995 events in certain places, including Gorazde and Bihac. With respect to the attachment in the pre-trial brief of General Rose's summary, there's reference to Gorazde, but not to Bihac, and we don't feel that that constitutes adequate notice that these events would be part of this trial. The indictment, itself, is defective in not providing any notice, and we don't believe that the references in the pre-trial brief are clear, consistent, and unequivocal enough such that we would have been put on notice that those events would be part of this trial. Secondly, with respect to relevance, even if it is believed that we did have sufficient notice, we'd ask the Court to exercise its discretion to exclude the evidence on the grounds of relevance. This is the first domino in a row which you have before you. If you admit evidence of Gorazde and Bihac, then we'll need time for cross-examination of that evidence, we'll need to do our own Defence investigation, you're likely to hear Defence witnesses. We'll be dealing with it in our closing submissions. You'll have to deal with it in the judgement, and it could be a point of appeal by either side. So when you flick the first domino today in deciding whether or not to admit the testimony of General Rose on these issues, it creates -- will set off the rest of those dominos that will have an impact on the scope and the length of the trial. So for those reasons, I would ask that you exclude the evidence from the amalgamated statement and also not allow any oral testimony about those subjects. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether it will be for Mr. Tieger or Ms. Edgerton to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll begin with the response, in any case, Your Honour, if I may. And I'd like to address first the issues of relevance. But I'd just like to note, Your Honours, in our submission, that at paragraphs 104, 106 and 107, which Mr. Robinson has referred to as incorporating the Gorazde evidence, are not, in fact, related to Gorazde and, therefore, outside of the scope of his objections, and, in fact, the relevance is obvious on their face. They do largely relate to Sarajevo. There's a couple of issues almost being conflated here, and I want to, in my response, initially underscore that the evidence cited by Mr. Robinson as being objectionable doesn't represent any kind of an expansion of the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution, as Mr. Robinson has indicated, doesn't charge or allege crimes occurred in the course of the Gorazde offensive, or Bihac later in 1994, but this evidence is being offered in relation to key aspects of the indictment against Dr. Karadzic in regard to -- and I'm going to go through those. In regard to both the Gorazde and Bihac offensives, this evidence is relevant to and demonstrates Dr. Karadzic's command and effective control over the VRS forces during the period of the indictment. As regards the Gorazde offensive, this evidence, in our submission, gives meaning to the implementation of the third strategic objective, the elimination of the Drina as a border separating Serbian states, and Dr. Karadzic's -- it's also relevant to Dr. Karadzic's intent, in the implementation of that objective, to permanently remove non-Serbs from Serb-claimed territory in the Drina Valley. In the objection, it's as though Mr. Robinson would have you view the events in the eastern enclaves, in particular Srebrenica 1995, in isolation, but I think it's inappropriate to do so, geographically or temporally. The evidence of the policies of the Bosnian Serb leadership toward the enclaves of Gorazde and Zepa, a policy of military attacks, blockade and convoy restrictions, is also relevant because that same pattern was applied to Srebrenica. All three of these enclaves were viewed almost as a package by the Bosnian Serb leadership. And in our submission, the removal of all three was vital for the successful implementation of that third strategic objective. And in a minute, I'll mention some documents where we can see that, but just to go further on the issue of relevance, this evidence is relevant to the UN hostage-taking that Dr. Karadzic's stands indicted for in May of 1995. It's relevant in that in the -- it's relevant in what General Rose describes as a pattern throughout 1994, a pattern of detaining UN and other humanitarian forces to stop NATO intervention, a pattern that repeated itself in May of 1995. And, additionally, in regards to Bihac, the evidence is relevant to the Prosecution's articulated theory as regards Sarajevo, that events elsewhere in the theatre affected the safety and security conditions for the civilians of the city of Sarajevo. Just to go to some of those documents that I mentioned, not even, Your Honours, did the Bosnian Serb leaders consider events in Gorazde to the exclusion of the other enclaves, and I'd like to recall a couple to Your Honours: P976, Directive 4, from 19 November 1992, called for the forces of the Drina Corps to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population. 65 ter 03979, a Drina Corps order number 2-126 from November 1992, in paragraph 1, called for the Drina Corps units to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, break them up, or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde. P977, Directive 5 from 25 June 1993 called for the Drina Corps to keep the remaining Muslim forces in Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica under constant siege and encirclement. P838, Directive 7, dated 8 March 1995, under the tasks of the Drina Corps was included the directive to create an unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope for further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa, and to liberate Serbian areas in the Gorazde enclave and reduce the enclave to the size of a protected area of three kilometres from the town center. And, finally, P01412, Dr. Karadzic's own words at the 52nd Assembly Session. At page 111, he said: "The time had come, and I signed Directive 7 to capture Teocak, Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde. The directive was signed, and we embarked on it." At page 112 in the same session, he said: "We were not able to take Gorazde at that time, and we're still unable to conquer it because the threats are serious and we cannot afford to punch them in the eye right now, but there will be the right time to take Gorazde, just as there was the right time to conquer Srebrenica." Your Honour, the same policies apply for all three eastern enclaves, Gorazde, Zepa and Srebrenica, and the strategic significance of an attack on one is, in our submission, not fully or fairly appreciated without evidence of the offensives on the other enclaves. So on the issue of relevance, I think those are my submissions, Your Honour. I should note that Dr. Karadzic received this statement of General Rose's in the summer of 2009. The 92 ter notification for this witness referring to this statement was initially filed on 23rd July 2010. A final notification of exhibits to be used with the witness, which substantially reduced the number of exhibits in the initial notification, was filed on 23 September 2010. In our submission, Your Honour, notice was, in fact, ample and there is no prejudice suffered by Dr. Karadzic in that regard. And on the issue of time for cross-examination, in my submission, Your Honour, it's almost inappropriate for the Defence to dictate the Prosecution's evidence in a case against him based on how he views the amount of time able -- or available to him for cross-examination, Your Honour. And unless Mr. Tieger has something additional to raise, I think I've dealt with all the points that Mr. Robinson has identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. May I have just a brief moment for a reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Dealing with the issue of notice first, I think the jurisprudence is clear that witness statements don't serve to correct or rectify a defect in the indictment, and you have to look to the opening statement and the pre-trial brief for sources for that, and I've indicated already the extent to which these events were dealt with in those documents. So the fact that we received General Rose's witness statement is not relevant to the issue of notice. With regard to the issue of relevance, the Prosecution argues that they need this evidence to show command and control, to show intent to permanently remove Muslims, and to show -- to prove their case of hostage-taking in 1995. They've charged Dr. Karadzic with events in 20 municipalities, as well as Sarajevo and Srebrenica, so do they really need this evidence? And if they do, it should have been in the indictment. And so it's our submission, based on the comments that we all heard and made on the 3rd of September at the status conference, that this presents an issue in which the Trial Chamber should exercise its discretion in the management of the case and should exclude the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Clearly, the events that happened in Gorazde and Bihac were not charged by the indictment. In that sense, the events in Gorazde and Bihac might not be germane to the charges in the indictment; however, the Chamber is of the view that they unquestionably provide background support for several issues contained therein, such as command and control, effective control, intent, et cetera, and pattern, et cetera. So in that sense, we find -- the Chamber finds the lines of questioning or the evidence proffered in the 92 ter statement relevant, and we do not accept your argument, Mr. Robinson. We'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for your inconvenience. There was something we had to discuss in your absence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. For the record, could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Hugh Michael Rose.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, do you recall giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And subsequent to this, you testified for the Prosecutor in the trial against Stanislav Galic --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in June of 2002?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You appeared as a witness at the ICJ on behalf of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I was a witness of the Court. I made the point very clear that I was not a witness for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you've written a book on your experiences in Bosnia and Herzegovina, called "Fighting For Peace"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I see you have brought a copy of your book with you. I take it that's for reference?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is for reference purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in January of last year, do you recall meeting with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, myself included, and preparing a statement consolidating elements of the evidence we've just discussed, including elements of your book?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I well remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in preparing to testify today, have you had the opportunity to review that statement and the associated documents referenced within the statement, itself?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I please just draw your attention -- and I see you have a document -- you've brought a document in with you, General. Is that a copy of the statement we've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could draw your attention to two paragraphs of that statement; 150 and 151. And that's, Your Honours, for the record, 65 ter 22285.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've found those paragraphs, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, both those paragraphs refer to events in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It should read "September 1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In both cases?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: In both cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, apart from those two it would appear to be typographical errors, do you have any other corrections or clarifications to make to this document?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Should you be asked the same questions today which gave rise to the answers in this written evidence, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: To the best of my ability, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honours, could I tender 65 ter 22285 as the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to read now a summary of the written evidence of General Rose, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General Sir Michael Rose was the commander of the United Nations forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina from January 1994 until January 1995. Upon his arrival in Sarajevo, he observed a city that had been "reduced to an almost medieval state, with no lights, water, or electricity." He was briefed that a number of civilians had been killed from shelling and sniping in the preceding weeks and months. Civilians, including children, continued to be killed by shelling in late January and early February. When General Rose raised the issue of indiscriminate shelling with Mr. Karadzic in a meeting on 30 January 1994, Mr. Karadzic described the continued shelling of the city as senseless and said he agreed it should stop. General Rose observed that by 1994, the Bosnian Serb leadership were keenly interested in a global or Bosnia-wide cease-fire as a means of freezing the confrontation lines and cementing their territorial gains, which equated at that time to about 70 per cent of the country. After the shelling of the Markale Market on 5 February 1994, General Rose moved quickly to implement a cease-fire in Sarajevo by establishing a 20-kilometre total exclusion zone for heavy weapons. The cease-fire was largely effectively implemented by both sides and remained in place for a large part of the remaining year. General Rose viewed the political leaders' ability to implement this cease-fire as indicative of their control over the military around Sarajevo. In April 1994, the Bosnian Serbs launched an offensive in Gorazde which eventually led to NATO air-strikes. In response, the Bosnian Serbs took UNPROFOR personnel hostage, a response that would repeat itself on other occasions during General Rose's tour. General Rose opined that the offensive was intended to squeeze the enclave and thereby put further pressure on the Bosnians to accept a global cease-fire. He also viewed the episode as an example of the effectively functioning relationship between the political and military arms of the Bosnian Serb leadership. General Rose frequently met with Mr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership. During such meetings, he regularly raised issues of sniping, freedom of movement, and access for humanitarian convoys. General Rose observed that the Bosnian Serbs appeared to block humanitarian aid or utilities as a means of achieving political ends or in response to events such as Bosnian Army offensives occurring elsewhere. At one meeting in September 1994, Mr. Karadzic complained about Security Council sanctions and said that: "If the international community treats us like a beast, then we will behave like a beast," referring to the control of utilities as a means of war. Despite the cease-fire in Sarajevo, sniping remained a feature of daily life. In August 1994, however, the leaderships of both warring factions acceded to an anti-sniping agreement. This was immediately followed by a marked decrease in sniping over the following weeks. Towards the end of 1994, the situation in Sarajevo and Bosnia generally deteriorated, with an increase in shelling and sniping incidents in Sarajevo and noticeable restrictions on utilities and the flow of humanitarian aid until a cessation of hostilities agreement was signed by the parties under the auspices of Former President Jimmy Carter on 31 December 1994. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I've been unable to log in to my LiveNote up until this point, and I just took the advantage of the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It takes time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to go into some areas of evidence or amplify some areas of evidence that you referred to in your written evidence that's now been filed. The first topic relates to meetings and negotiations. Your written evidence indicates you had frequent meetings with the political and military leadership of the warring factions, both on the ground and outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At what military and command or political level were your interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, we were talking to the top political and military leadership of the so-called, at the time, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was that, in particular?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, on the political side, you had Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, from time to time Mr. Zametica. And on the military side it was always General Mladic and Colonel Tolimir, who was his military assistant, sometimes accompanied by one or two other military figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of the matters discussed at these meetings, was there any differentiation depending on the location of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were always two levels at which we discussed things. The first one was the discussions that revolved around trying to bring an end to the war; i.e., the process of cease-fire, cessation of hostilities, and, finally, the bringing about of a permanent peace. And at the next level, it was the running of United Nations High Commission for Refugee convoys across Bosnia. And, of course, the UNHCR or HCR, as the French like to call it, was feeding all three parties -- people of all three parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then as a result of your interaction or encounters discussing these different issues, did you then develop an overview of the political/military situation in the country?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the overall political/military situation in Bosnia, which really lasted throughout 1994, was the -- on the Serb side, there was a desire to bring an end to the war. As things stood, they controlled, as you already said, most of the territory. They were clearly wishing to trade territory for peace on their terms; i.e., they wanted the bits of Bosnia they wanted. They were prepared to give up bits, either to the Croat side or the Bosnian government side, the bits they didn't want. They -- from the Bosnian government side, and most of the time because of the agreement between the Croatians and the Muslim side to form a federation, there were two sides to the conflict for most of 1994. On the Bosnian government side, who headed the federation, there was a desire not to allow the gains -- territorial gains that had been made by the Bosnian Serb side in the first two years of the war to be turned into a peace. And, therefore, initially the Bosnian government had welcomed the arrival of the United Nations and its ability to deliver aid and alleviate suffering, but as time went on, they started to object to the second purpose of the United Nations' presence, which was to bring about peace, because they wanted to go back to war in order to recover their lost territories by war. That was the general strategic position which was prevailing throughout 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of overall territorial control, then, you've alluded to the Bosnian Serbs having approximately 70 -- control of approximately 70 per cent of the former republic, then does it follow that the Bosnian forces controlled a much smaller portion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: A much smaller portion, which I don't know the percentages of, but, of course, the Croat -- the Croats controlled most of the southern parts and some of the western parts of Bosnia, and the Muslim side really the central section, with little bits here and there, like Gorazde or Srebrenica, Bihac, but mainly in the areas around Sarajevo, probably with a split. It was about 15 per cent/15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there a change or a transformation in the strategic situation over the course of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: A massive change. What happened in 1994 was that the -- in February/March, the federation was formed between the Croatians and the Muslims under the Washington Accord, and this tilted the military balance against the Bosnian Serb side. The reason was, of course, that the Bosnian federation started to build its military capability, and as they built military capability, so the long lines -- the extended lines that the Bosnian Serb side had to maintain, it became weakened. Their control of these lines became weak, particularly with the sanctions that started to bite against former Yugoslavia. And, therefore, they had reached, in military terms, I mean, Klausewitz was the first person to call it the culminating point. And from that moment onwards, from March 1994, the Bosnian Serbs were inevitably going to be in a weakening situation, whilst the Bosnian federation was going to be in a strengthening situation, and the balance at some point would flip, completely to the advantage of the federation. And there was also an increasing feeling that at some point NATO would become involved. And, of course, once NATO became involved actively, then the balance would be tilted even further in favour of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did this transformation, or the culminating point, as you've described it, have any relationship to the positions taken at international peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It most certainly did, because, of course, the Bosnian federation became more encouraged in their strategy of not signing up to any peace accord which they felt was unjust and rewarded the aggressor, and, of course, they had the support of NATO, and the Americans in particular, in that position. And the Bosnian Serbs, I think, began to understand, slowly but surely, that at some point they would lose their military and territorial advantage. And that inevitably affected the debate because, of course, the Bosnian Serbs would become more desperate to get peace on their terms as time went on. I hope that makes logical sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Very much. Thank you. In your function and as a result of these meetings and negotiations, did you develop any understanding of the war aims of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb leadership, as I say, was to bring about peace on their terms before the military situation started to deteriorate too greatly, and, of course, it was to use their military advantage at that time to lever the Bosnian pressure -- the Bosnian government into making an earlier peace than the Bosnian government would have wished to have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you learn of their territorial aspirations or objectives?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes. It became clear that, through discussions reported to us not only from the contact group and other intermediaries but also our own discussions, that the sort of figure that the Bosnian Serbs were prepared to reduce their territorial holdings down to, from 70 per cent, was probably to 51 per cent, but, of course, the real debate was about the quality of the territory that they were going to trade. And if you measure the 70/30 per cent difference, much of that 30 per cent was empty territory which was of no use, anyway, to the Serbs, and the debate really came about -- became focused on the Posavina corridor, bits of Western Bosnia would remain Muslim, what bits of Sarajevo would remain Serb or Muslim, and they were the sort of critical elements. There was the power-generating plant to the south of Sarajevo, the right to run railways and roads through each other's territory, and lots of detail, but that was the general feeling, that the Bosnian Serbs would accept a 51/49 per cent in their favour, given, in their view, the vital bits of territory that they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you aware what you describe as those vital bits of territory that they wanted might be?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Not in any great detail. But, for example, in Sarajevo we always had the feeling that they wanted to maintain their ownership of the Grbavica area, which was still Serb held.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And apart from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think they certainly wanted Srebrenica to be wholly Serb, probably all that side of Bosnia to be Serb. Whether they were -- would concede on Gorazde or not, we never discovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the topics discussed during your meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, you referred to support of UNHCR in their delivery of humanitarian aid. What priority did you give that in your -- in UNPROFOR's mandate?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the UNPROFOR mandate, which was revisited when I first arrived, as a result of a meeting I had in New York with Mr. Kofi Annan, who at that was head of the peace-keeping mission, we decided that there were three main areas which we should focus on, based on the sometimes conflicting United Nations Security Council resolutions which had been passed successively over the years in response to different crises. They were: The primary role, to continue and improve the delivery of humanitarian aid to the 2.7 million people who were daily dependent on that aid at the beginning of 1994 in Bosnia. And, of course, they were people from all three sides but mainly the Muslim side, living in the enclaves. The second purpose of the presence of the United Nations peace-keepers was to try and create the conditions in which there could be a political resolution of conflict by lowering the level of conflict and allowing discussion to take place, political discussion. And, finally, and this was the understated aim, was to stop the war from spreading into the neighbouring territories of Macedonia or Montenegro, which was a live possibility at the time. But the primary aim of the presence of the United Nations remained the facilitation of the delivery of humanitarian aid, and that was something which we would not allow to be deflected in our mission by other requirements placed upon us sometimes by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the situation was in 1994, in terms of UNPROFOR's ability to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the targets for the delivery of humanitarian aid were set partly by the World Health Organisation's understanding and surveys of the condition of the populations there and also by the UNHCR's observations, and, roughly, it measured some 2.000 metric tonnes per day. And the United Nations Protection Force and the UNHCR were achieving nothing like that, I mean, to the breakdown of the roads, the systems, the blocking of the convoys sometimes by all three parties at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just referred to the blocking of the convoys sometimes by all three parties. Did you have any difficulty in that regard with the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Indeed. They were obviously -- because they were dominating, territorially, the country and holding a number of the enclaves under siege, they were the ones who were doing most of the blocking, particularly into Sarajevo. And there were times in Sarajevo in January when the warehouses -- the UN warehouses were empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you raised these difficulties with the Bosnian Serb leaders. Do you recall raising them with the accused, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: At practically every single meeting we had, there was always discussion about the movement of convoys. We also adopted a slightly more robust approach from the start, and early on we enforced the passage of a convoy into Sarajevo using the support of NATO close-air-support aircraft, and the convoy, which originally had been disallowed, ran. We had much freedom of movement after we had done that, less obstruction from the Serb side and, indeed, the other sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could turn to a document which is referenced in your written evidence at paragraph 182, 65 ter 06870, while we're on this subject. It's a report by Lieutenant-Colonel Jamie Daniell, dated 12th December 1994, about a meeting you had at Pale with Koljevic, Krajisnik, Tolimir, Gvero, and others.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I have that paragraph in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And shortly you should be able to see the image of that document on the screen in front of you. Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that we have difficulty in producing the document through e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour, and we should be able to resort to the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, can I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you see the document reflecting this meeting now on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention to paragraph 3 of this document, the subject of convoys, and in particular 3(b), where you are noted as stating that it was clear to you that the bureaucratic procedures and ridiculous questions which now accompanied convoy requests could only be imposed as a result of a conscious policy to derail the convoy system. This -- I'm sorry, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That was the situation at the time. I mean, the -- it was in the strategic interests, on the Serb side, not to allow these convoys to run, and thereby putting pressure on the Bosnian government. But, of course, they had signed up early on in the -- before the deployment of the UN Protection Force to the free movement of all convoys, and they were having to come out with different and innovative ideas about how to block these convoys. Often, this was done by physical blocking or attacking the convoys, but it was also sometimes done by ridiculous and absurd bureaucratic procedures, which took an awful lot of our time to have to deal with, and they would search some bit of -- a convoy, find some undeclared item - it might have been as small as a biscuit or something, and I'm giving an illustrative example - and the whole convoy would be turned back or refused passage. And it became a routine procedure on their part towards the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this document, in the next sentence you're noted as saying: "This policy was working well, since we were now at critical levels of fuel and food in a number of locations, and the BSA took every opportunity to steal anything which they considered wrongly manifested." And I'm wondering if you could explain what prompted the use of the word "policy" in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was systematic and could only have come as a decision from the top. My chief of staff, Major Row was ensuring the passage of the convoys and agreeing with the warring parties when and where these convoys would run, and then he would spend an inordinate amount of time after that trying to unstick the blocking of the convoys. And he was as aware as I was that this was a matter of policy by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you aware of any effect that this policy had on the situation, first, in the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It most certainly did. The people in Srebrenica, in particular, and Zepa were reduced to a level of near starvation. Gorazde was never quite so bad because it was easier to get to, but even then the situation became critical on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there UNPROFOR forces deployed in these areas at that time as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were, and they suffered great shortage as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You referred to this policy as -- and I'll just see if I can find your words. Your indulgence for a moment. You referred to this policy as relating to the strategy and being in support of the strategy of the Bosnian Serb forces. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, they were using the blocking of convoys to the enclaves as a means of putting pressure on the Bosnian government to sign up to peace on their terms, to try and gain some control over the United Nations psychologically, possibly, as well. They certainly were aware of the consequences of their actions in blocking these convoys because we brought it to their attention ceaselessly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was Sarajevo similarly affected?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Sarajevo was a slightly different situation, in that we had brought about a cessation of hostilities around Sarajevo in February of 1994 and the withdrawal of heavy weapons from around there, and as a result of that, the ability to run not only UNHCR convoys but straight ordinary commercial convoys from outside the enclave, which Sarajevo, of course, was, into Sarajevo became commonplace. And throughout the spring and summer, with the odd interruption, life started to return to normal in Sarajevo because it was being resupplied in a much more normal fashion than had happened hitherto. But in September 1994, all that came to an end when the Bosnian government side launched an attack against the Serb side, and the Serbs started to block the convoys again into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your written evidence, at paragraphs 127 to 129, you referred to an event somewhat earlier than that, the closure of the airport to commercial convoys using the road down Mount Igman; paragraphs 127 to 129. Have you found those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yeah, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you able to put this in context for us, this event?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think this was happening for two reasons: 1, that the pressure, again, not only strategically, needed to be brought to bear on the Bosnian government side to adopt their peace terms; but also to try and get them to sign up to the anti-sniper agreement; they also had a desire to have Sarajevo demilitarised. And I think they were the three areas which caused them to shut down the routes, because they could see that people now in Sarajevo on the Bosnian Muslim side were living far better than the people on the Bosnian Serb side, who, of course, were being -- suffered the sanctions that had been brought to bear by the -- on Belgrade by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, for your planning purpose, I wanted to let you know that we are minded to take the first break at quarter to 4.00 for half an hour. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Conditions in Sarajevo for the Bosnian Muslims and, I assume, others who lived within the city have been improved as a consequence of the February 1994 cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Those conditions dramatically improved, and for the first time the utilities started to be restored, the trams started to run again, water -- piped water, and the people of Sarajevo for the first time started to hope that this was the start of a return to normality for them and the end of the war. Hopes which, sadly, were to be dashed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall -- perhaps you could explain for us the significance, in terms of the supply of food and other aid to the city, of the ability to use the -- or to run the commercial convoys across the airport using the Igman Road. What did it represent for feeding the city and supplying the city?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think most of the commercial convoys, in fact, did not come through -- down the mountain. The road was too difficult to come down. If you like, it was the emergency route that could be used when the main routes were shut. Most of the routes came down the normal major road systems into Sarajevo. So the consequence of opening these routes was people there could buy fresh food, they could have fish that had come up from the coast that day. You started to see flower stores opening up. Things they hadn't seen for two and a half years started to become normality again for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What were the Blue Routes, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The Blue Routes were the routes which we had designated as being central to the resupply of Sarajevo, and I explained one of them came down Mount Igman, but it was only the one that was used in extremism. Most of them were not down Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to turn to a document, 65 ter 21913. But I should note this document, we cite it in paragraph 4 of our final notification, as it's a new document and not yet added on the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We admit it -- we grant it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we then call up that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you -- you should see the English version on the screen shortly in front of you. Thank you. General, before you, you see a document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska, dated 23 July 1994, to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps commander, on preparing units to prevent the transit across the Sarajevo Airport, a preparatory order. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I note that this document, in the first paragraph, states: "Pursuant to an oral order of the president of the Republika Srpska and in order to carry out the necessary preparations for the prevention of transit across the Butmir Airport ..." And then issues certain directions. Do you see that opening paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does this document, to your mind, have any relationship to the closure of the Blue Routes and the closure of the airport to the commercial convoys using the Igman Road referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it matches very much the results that we saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you infer anything from the reference to an oral order of the president of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it confirms the view that we always had, that there was a very close relationship at the top between the military and the civil authority on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1639, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And by my notes, I have forgotten to make the same request for the earlier document, 65 ter 06870.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as P1640.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, we've talked -- and you've mentioned the cease-fire in February of 1994, and I wonder if you can comment on the effectiveness of that cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the cease-fire was arranged at a meeting at the airport. And after a certain amount of difficulty in implementing it, because it had to be proved to NATO that the Bosnian Serbs had withdrawn all their heavy weapons from outside a 20-kilometre circle around Sarajevo, and, of course, the United Nations, which is a peacekeeping force, doesn't have intelligence-gathering capability, but, of course, does have United Nations Military Observers, some of whom are not particularly suited for that sort of work, we were able to assure NATO that all the weapons had been withdrawn. And the co-ordination of that withdrawing of weapons could only have come as a result of a political decision being passed to the military. Of course, both sides cheated greatly on this withdrawal of heavy weapons and hid some of their heavy weapons within that 20-kilometre circle and did not hand them in to the United Nations weapon-collecting point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We discovered -- we discovered them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, given that, we could turn to the second document we had -- we've referred to in our final notification, paragraph 4, 65 ter 22945 - this is also a document not yet added to the Prosecution's 65 ter list - with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see a document on the screen before you, General, dated 10 February 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- entitled "Proposal for setting aside artillery"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I invite you to scan, because this is a document of more than one page, the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I've done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could we move on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, this document is a proposal for the setting aside of inoperative artillery pieces received from other VRS corps and the camouflaging of others, you see on this page, including 122-millimetre Howitzers. Please advise when you've been able to scan this second page.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move on to the final page of the translation, please, and page 2 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've read this document now, General. Do you have any comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it conforms very much to what we thought was happening on the ground. But since the United Nations at that time was working with three partners, albeit recalcitrant partners, towards peace, they did not have, as I say, intelligence-gathering capability. Although we may have suspected that this was happening, we did not have the capability of searching every building, hangar, bit of ground in that 20-kilometre-radius circle, to see whether our suspicions were true or not. On occasions, we came across them, hidden weapons, and insisted on them being moved into the weapon-collecting point. But the key point was that the firing of shells into Sarajevo did stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you take anything -- having read this document, do you take anything from this document in terms of the Serb forces' effective control of their heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, there was extreme co-ordination between the front-line and the upper echelons of the political/military structure, and the decisions taken at the top would be reflected immediately on the ground, as one would expect in any army. And one must remember that the Bosnian Serb Army was the rump or the Serb elements -- Bosnian Serb elements of the regular Yugoslav Army and, therefore, had all the same mechanisms of communication and disciplines built into their structure. It would have been surprising had that not been the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask this be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1641, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, you've commented on the fact that fire around Sarajevo effectively stopped. And in your written evidence, at paragraph 45, you describe a walk you took with Sector Sarajevo Commander Soubirou across the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo bridge as a test of the effectiveness of the cease-fire. I'd like to take you to a document of that same date, please, 65 ter 21218. General, this is an order from Dragomir Milosevic directing the implementation of the cease-fire on the Sarajevo front, based on a letter of the VRS Main Staff. Could you have a read through this document and let us know when you've got to the bottom of this first page.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page, please, which contains the translation of the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on this document in relation to the situation that day?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, events on the ground conform exactly to this instruction by the Bosnian Serb military. And, indeed, the Bosnian government side did continue to fire at them, but they didn't respond, and the Bosnian government forces stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you infer anything from this as to the Bosnian Serb forces' effective control over the use of their heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolute control.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be admitted as the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1642 -- P1642, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, what was people's reaction to the cease-fire, the people that you spoke to and saw within the city?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: People were elated. They -- I would have saw their children coming out from cellars, where they had been hiding for the past two years, and playing football in the street. As I say, they for the first time became hopeful that there would be a permanent end to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, rather than moving on to a further topic, and noting the time, I wonder if you would care to pause now. Otherwise, I'm fully prepared to continue, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some members of the Chamber should go to the meeting for half an hour from quarter to 4.00, so if you could carry on for a further five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the subject, General, of a football game, I'd like to take you to paragraph 64 of your written evidence, where you described a football match played between the United Nations and the Sarajevo team on 20 March 1994, and the fact that Dr. Karadzic gave an undertaking that the match would be allowed to go ahead without interruption. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I recall it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where is that stadium located, to your recollection, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: In the center of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that stadium in sight and range, to your knowledge, of Bosnian Serb infantry and heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the match take place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It took place without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I know it's a long time after the fact, but could you hazard a guess as to the attendance figures?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: 10.000, maybe, 20. I don't know. I'm not a football [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say that the match took place without interruption, does that include without interruption by any single shelling or sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was zero incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did this signify anything to you, in terms of Dr. Karadzic's effective control over the use of weapons by his forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes. He -- Dr. Karadzic was as good as his word and made sure that the match could go ahead without any sniping or shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we see, then, 65 ter 06667, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you see before you a translation of a document signed by Dr. Karadzic, dated 19 March 1994, to General Galic. Do you remember who General Galic was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: He was commanding the corps surrounding that part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document informs General Galic that Dr. Karadzic has given permission for a football match to be played, and directs him that during the time the match is to be played, it's necessary to prevent the Serbian side from provoking an incident, and General Galic is to inform the brigades that they shall absolutely comply with this order. Do you have any comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it conforms, once again, to the events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask for this to be the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1643.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now shall we take the break, Ms. Edgerton? As indicated, we'll take a break until quarter past 4.00, for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on to another topic, General Rose, I'd like to deal with sniping. And perhaps you can tell us about -- or perhaps I could ask you to tell us about your observations of the dangers posed by sniping for civilians within government-held -- Bosnian-government-held Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the presence of snipers, of course, made normal life impossible in Sarajevo. The fear of being shot by a sniper prevented all normal life, and people could, in effect, only come out at night or in areas they knew couldn't be covered by snipers, to go about their normal business. And there was a climate of fear which existed until the sniper agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you comment on the effectiveness, as you observed it, of the sniper agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, initially I think it worked quite well, but after that it was patchy and there was always breakdowns on both sides. But, nevertheless, the situation did improve after the 14th of August, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you infer anything from that improvement as to the effective control of snipers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was definitely -- sniping was part of the policy of intimidating the civilian population, and therefore there was clear control over the sniping that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to take you, on the question of sniping, to paragraphs 155 and 156 of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Edgerton. Excuse me, General. You said you always saw the breakdowns on both sides, and later you said sniping was part of the policy of intimidating the civilian population. Do you refer to a specific side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was referring at that point to the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, of course, there was sniping the other way into Grbavica and elsewhere which, presumably, the Bosnian government were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps on that note, just to go back to my question as to the effective control of the snipers, did that apply to both factions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It did, although it was less tidy, I think, than the heavy artillery bombardment which had taken place, which stopped absolutely. The sniping was a sort of untidy business and it never really properly ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraphs 155 and 156 of your written evidence, you referred to a meeting you attended along with Mr. Andreev, General Gobillard, and others, with General Mladic on 10 October 1994. And in paragraph 155, you refer to a document -- a fax from Mr. Andreev to Mr. de Mello, reporting on the meeting, and I'd like to show you that document. It's P00867. It appears now, General, on the screen in front of you, the first page. If I could invite you to have a look through that and familiarise yourself with the document. And tell us when you've done, and we can then move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I've done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 of this document, you are recorded as condemning an incident that Saturday in which a tram was shot at. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you -- to what extent did you bring protests like this or notice like this to the Bosnian Serb leadership about sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, when a serious incident occurred, we always raised it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what, if any, responses did you tend to receive?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, initially, we, of course, protested strongly against the sniping, and their reply was along the lines, normally, that, of course, It wasn't us that carried out the sniping, it was the Bosnian Muslims who were trying to incriminate us and destroy our reputation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I note in this instance you're recorded, in paragraph 5, as receiving a similar response. However, an UNPROFOR technical expert present was able to assure the party that the shooting did not come from the Holiday Inn side. A map was provided.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That, indeed, was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This incident, then, General, deals with the sniping of a tram. Do you -- or could you tell us as to whether there was any significance to the restoration of the tram operations under your or during your period of command?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the restoration of the tram system was greatly welcomed by the people of Sarajevo, who had been forced hitherto to take long, devious routes to avoid either sniping or shelling, and they were always at risk. And the fact that they could now travel on the trams heralded a brighter future for them, more safe existence, and so it was something which greatly lifted the spirits of Sarajevo, having their trams back.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To what extent was the operation of those trams, during your tour and to the best of your recollection, affected by situations of sniping or shelling?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: What normally happened when a tram was sniped at was that the service would be withdrawn for a day or two, and then it would be reinstated after we had protested, and they would run again for a period of time until the next sniping incident. But the people of Sarajevo were remarkably resilient, and as one lady put it to me, an elderly lady, it is better to be shot dead on a tram than when you are hobbling along a two-mile stretch of street.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What did she mean -- what did you understand her to mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, she was forced to go down this long road daily to get her supplies, and she would rather go in a comfortable manner than in an uncomfortable manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That document could be removed from the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could just go forward a bit to paragraph 156, General. In fact, it appears like there were two incidents that drew your attention at around this time; not only the firing on the tram referred to in the previous paragraph, but a second incident involving fire at two women in the Sarajevo suburb of Vojkovici. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall writing any correspondence as a result of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I wrote protests to both Dr. Karadzic and President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 01302, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise -- this is a two-page document. Do you recognise the first page you see in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's that, then?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is a letter I wrote to President Izetbegovic, in protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this -- well, perhaps I could deal with the second page of this document before I move on. Could we move on to page 2, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise page 2 of this document, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do. It's a letter I wrote to Dr. Karadzic, in similar protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have this document as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1644.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, over the course of your service in Sarajevo, did you develop a view as to the objectives behind the shelling, sniping, and blockade of the city, as to the Bosnian Serbs' objectives?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes. It was clearly to put pressure on the Bosnian government to bring about a peace deal on the Bosnian Serb terms; i.e., something that was favourable to the Bosnian Serbs, not to the Bosnian government side. But an incident like the sniping we just referred to would have happened very much in response to other events, specific events. For example, there had been an incursion on Mount Igman by the Bosnian Army across the demilitarised zone, which had resulted in the killing of 20 Serb military nurses, and the sniping that took place the next day or the day after was very much in response to that and caused a similar response from the Bosnian government side. So nothing was -- no event was isolated in itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you. Just to go back to the first part of your answer about -- that the shelling, sniping, and blockade was to put pressure on the Bosnian government to bring about a peace deal on Bosnian Serb terms, could you tell us what the basis for that view is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it was the view taken, the result of the strategic overall situation that occurred in that country at that moment in 1994. As I said, the military balance was tilting against the Bosnian Serb side, so it was in their interest to agree on peace. The Bosnian government side refused to agree on peace, and, therefore, all these actions were strategically designed to bring pressure to bear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to another area that you dealt with in your written evidence, that of Gorazde, I wonder if, similarly, you have a view as to the objective of the offensive on the town in April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it was clearly the result of that line of thinking. There had been discussions at the airport between the two sides, mediated by the United Nations, suggesting that we should move, after the cease-fire around Sarajevo, to a full cessation of hostility, leading ultimately to a permanent peace. There had been a greater desire, inevitably, from the Bosnian Serb side for that peace than there was from the government side, and discussions broke out about which order this should take place in; i.e., should there be a cease-fire agreed for the rest of the country before a final cessation of hostilities or should there be a cessation of hostilities which should include a cease-fire? And while this discussion was going on, the Bosnian Serb side launched an attack into Gorazde, the safe area of Gorazde, as a way of putting pressure on the Bosnian Serb -- the Bosnian government. The secondary aim, of course, was to recover the Serb ground which they had lost in the fighting in 1992 and 1993 on the right side of the river which flows through Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your written evidence, at paragraph 85, it's noted that on 11 April 1994, you told General Mladic he had 10 minutes to halt tanks advancing on Gorazde, and shortly before the dead-line the JCOs reported tanks had turned around. Have you found that entry?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you infer anything from the immediacy of the reaction following your warning?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was clear there was a very, very close connection between the high commander and what was happening on the front-line, down to the individual tank. I mean, it may have been a coincidence, but we thought it was more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can just go a little bit further on the same page, to paragraph 87, there it refers to a document, 65 ter 08055, also dated 11 April 1994, from a Colonel Dragisa Masal. And I'll just wait for a few moments until it comes up on the screen. Thank you. First of all, General, are you familiar with this Colonel Dragisa Masal?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes. We dealt with him after the cessation of the fighting around Gorazde, and it appeared, from what we understood, that he was the commander of the units on the right bank of the river, the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at its last paragraph, number 7, this document notes that Colonel Masal is forwarding a message from the commander of the Glavni stab VRS, General Mladic, "who visited our zone of combat operations on 10 April 1994," and then says, in quotes: "Keep pushing energetically onwards, pay no attention to what is going on around us. The Turks must disappear from these areas." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on this passage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it conforms very much to the events that took place on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does it affect, in any way, your views as to the objectives of this operation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No. I was surprised to hear, from the last reference in that letter, that the aim had been to clear all the Bosnian Muslims out of the Gorazde -- if that's what it meant, but we always thought that they were merely intent on clearing them from the right bank, not crossing into the main part of Gorazde and clearing all the Muslims out of there, although that subsequently, it turned out, may have been the case. So I don't quite know what that line refers to, when he says "these areas -- the Turks must disappear from these areas." My suspicion is it refers to the right bank, rather than the main part of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be admitted as the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just moving on in your written evidence: At paragraph 90, you refer to the detention of UN soldiers, aid workers, and UNMOs on 14 April 1994, following a second round of air-strikes. Paragraph 90.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You commented that this came to be a recognisable pattern of behaviour on the part of the Serbs, and I'd like to ask you: In what way did it become a pattern? What did you mean to explain by using that word?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It became the immediate knee-jerk reaction to any air-strikes or any other form of coercion that we exercised against the Serbs. For example, I think the firing by the Danish tanks against Serb tanks resulted in the blocking of convoys and the taking of hostages. So it was their knee-jerk reaction to any use of force by the United Nations Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On -- when you use the word "pattern," then, and based on what you've just described, do you -- does that refer to this reaction repeating itself?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It repeated itself not only throughout 1994, but as we know in well-publicised incidents, into 1995 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For those incidents that took place during the course of your command, do you recall how widespread -- how geographically widespread they might have been when they took place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it didn't matter where the hostage-taking occurred, but it was always related to some use of force by the UN in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we see -- oh, your indulgence for a moment, please. I need to find a 65 ter number. Could we please see P00855, please, a document dated 19 April 1994, from General Mladic, sent to the corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this document, please, General, and let us know when you've had an opportunity to scan it.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, I've scanned it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document notes, in the preface paragraph -- or orders, and begins with -- is an order, and begins with the first line: "Based on the verbal order of the RS president ..." And goes down to paragraph 4: "Immediately increase measures for the security and control of UNPROFOR and international humanitarian organisations. In the event of massive air-raids against RS units and facilities, disarm and arrest them immediately, confiscate their weapons and combat equipment, and use them for," it says here, "anti-aircraft warfare." That's an order by General Mladic. Now, from this document -- or do you see any relationship between this document and the detention of UNPROFOR and other international humanitarian representatives that took place in April?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it clearly correlates exactly with our view that this was likely to be an immediate reaction of the Bosnian Serb side in response to any UN or NATO air-strikes or other forms of use of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you infer anything from this document, or having read this document, as to the nature of the control over these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, again, it's obvious that, as in any military force, the orders that are given at the top are obeyed by all ranks below.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We could remove that document from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, earlier on we talked, in a rather detailed fashion, about the question of freedom of movement and how important that was to UNPROFOR's mission on the ground. And in that regard, I'd like to take you to paragraph 92 of your written evidence, where you looked at a document dated 15 April 1994, 65 ter 08329. And you should see that on the screen in front of you fairly shortly. It's a report from General Milovanovic to the president of the republic and others. Who did you know General -- or who was General Milovanovic, General Rose; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think he was one of the generals who was either on the staff, to start with, and then ended up as a commander in the field of the Bosnian Serb Army on that side of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 4, I think, of the English translation, paragraph 4 of this document. No, page 4. I'm mistaken. Perhaps page 5. Your indulgence for a moment. Uh-huh, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention to paragraph 3 at the bottom of the page, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the notation about halfway down the paragraph to the effect that: "In other parts of the RS, there were no movements of humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys, meaning that the order of the Supreme Command and the commander of the Main Staff of the Army/RS has been fully implemented"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you infer from this document anything as regards to the freedom of movement of -- the control of the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR convoys?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It's quite clear that this action or order was given in response to the NATO air-strikes, and the whole of the delivery of humanitarian aid programme was -- had to be abandoned by the UN as a result of this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go to the next sentence in this paragraph, which notes: "In the evening hours, as ordered by the president of the republic, we temporarily ceased combat operations and ensured departure of two UNPROFOR helicopters from the area of Gorazde, where they allegedly pulled out two wounded members of British forces."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That, again, correlates to what happened on the ground. Tragically, a member of the United Nations forces in Gorazde was killed by Serb fire and another injured, and Mr. Akashi, the SRSG, happened to be in Pale at the time, negotiating a cease-fire to the fighting around Gorazde, and prevailed upon Dr. Karadzic to call a halt to the fighting while these soldiers were evacuated out, the dead one and the injured one. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have this, please, as the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1646, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, prior to coming here to testify today, did you have occasion to review some -- the translations of note-books that belonged to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you find those note-books to correspond roughly to the period of your command in UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
