utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On reviewing those note-books, did you find -- have occasion to find entries related to meetings you, yourself, had with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Generally speaking, did you find the entries as regards those meetings to correspond to the evidence in your statement and reports prepared on those meetings, UNPROFOR reports?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Obviously, they were written from an entirely different perspective and possibly were far less comprehensive than the UN reports of those meetings, but, nevertheless, they generally corresponded with our understanding of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to take you, General, to a couple of entries from one of those note-books, P01486, a note-book that runs from April until September 1994; English, page 29, and B/C/S, page 34. And the entry we're going to dates from 23 April 1994, relating to a meeting of the Supreme Command. Oh, I'm sorry. When I gave the B/C/S citations, I gave the citations from the original Cyrillic version rather than the Latin transcript, and I was referring to the e-court pages. Whoops. The English page is fine. General, do you see the entry I've just described in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do, and I've scanned them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the notation relating to Dr. Karadzic, which says that: "The operation has been very well planned and carried out. More has been taken than planned"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have an appropriate page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 34 -- e-court page 34 of this B/C/S version. And when I chose the pages, I was going by the actual e-court page, rather than the page number that's handwritten at the top. And I'm really sorry, I didn't think to note an ERN number for that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about going a further five pages? I note "29" and "24."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, if I could just direct you, below that notation attributed to Dr. Karadzic and a notation indicating "my" or General Mladic's presentation, do you see the notation which reads: "The Turks suffered military defeat near Gorazde and the Drina River Valley"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And referring to this, it continues: "They did not represent an organised military force in the enclaves of Srebrenica, Gorazde, Zepa which we must neutralise in the near future using political, economic, government and, if necessary, military and police measures"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, does this affect your assessment as to the objectives of the operation you've spoken about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Not really. The surprise is that they were not mentioning Bihac, because, of course, they actually attacked into Bihac before they did into Zepa or Srebrenica or, indeed, Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go further in this document, to page 46 in the English and page 56 of the original B/C/S version, we should see an entry for 7 May 1994: "In a place called Srbinje," we have it in English, thank you, "an analysis of the operation Zvijezda 1994." And I'll just wait until we get there in the original version before I move forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now that we've found the meeting and the date, if we could just go, again, a little bit further, to page 48 of the English, so two pages further in the English, and 58 in the B/C/S, two pages further in the B/C/S. General, do you see a notation similar to the previous one, which reads at the top of this page "My presentation," where General Mladic congratulates on results achieved in Operation Zvijezda 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we now go two pages over again in the English, to page 50, and in the B/C/S to page 60, part of the same presentation. I've done this just to place it for you in time and, to what extent I can, in context. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention to the bottom of this page 50, General, where we read: "We're not completely done with the M in the enclave of Gorazde. The enclave ..." And if we could go over to the next page. "... needs to be cut down, reduced, and made to suffer losses, especially on the outskirts, beyond a three-kilometre perimeter, and in this way ensure there is no perspective for the survival of the M in this area."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have a comment on this passage, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, it more or less aligns itself with what happened on the ground, once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does it affect your view as to the objectives of the operation in any way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No. Keeping pressure on the enclaves was always part of their strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, if you could tell us what this three-kilometre perimeter refers to, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, indeed, sir. It refers to an agreement that was struck by Mr. Akashi with the Bosnian Serb side about the withdrawal of heavy weapons and military units from a three-kilometre circle around Gorazde, in the way that we had achieved in Sarajevo early on. And this agreement, I think, was made in Belgrade, a meeting at which I did not attend, but, of course, was given the consequences of, and it was up to us on the ground to implement that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just your indulgence for a further moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You talked, at the beginning of your evidence-in-chief, General, about the -- what you understood to be the territorial objectives of the Bosnian Serbs during the course of your tour. Are you able to comment to any extent on the nature of that territory, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, no further than I've already described.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. To close, I'd like to just come back to Sarajevo very briefly, and I'd like to ask you the following: whether at any time, over the course of your tour in the city, did you assess there was any realistic prospect of a break-out of Sarajevo by the forces within the city.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No. The Bosnian Muslim Army was in no state to -- even though they were heavier in infantry or more numerous in infantry than the Serbs were, they were in no position to make a successful break-out from Sarajevo. They didn't have the equipment or the training or the heavy armour or artillery which would have been required there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That, Your Honours, concludes my evidence-in-chief. And before I take my seat, I wonder how Your Honours would prefer to deal with the matter of the associated documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are minded to tender all of them listed?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from Mr. Robinson, whether there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, other than to maintain our previous position that all of the associated exhibits related to Gorazde and Bihac ought to be excluded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will raise some issues related to a certain exhibit. First -- I will refer to the 65 ter number: 6850.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you, by any chance, have the same itemised list beside -- in front of you that I do? Because I have -- on our final notification, we had an updated filing that reflected -- I tried to give things item numbers so that it might speed up this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's item number 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Item number 14 is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- 6850. In his statement, I take it it's para 676. But he didn't make any comment on this, so we'll not admit this. And then -- you are not tendering the witness's earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you withdraw them?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, definitely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fine. How about 7496? Let me find it here, item --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Number 25, I have it, Your Honour, referred to in paragraph 98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On this item, as well, the witness didn't make any comment. All he said, he was shown this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The same is true with 7619. So if you are minded to tender it, probably you need to put it to the witness. So we'll not admit it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are not tendering his earlier transcript in Galic, just to confirm with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And item 14683, 14683, have we dealt with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, but I can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's appearing in para 97, but the witness didn't make any comment about this as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I be permitted to put this document to the witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, later on. And how about 14689? On this item either -- the witness didn't make any comments. So if you are minded to tender those two, you need to put them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just the first one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise, other items will be admitted. And if it is okay, instead of going into detail, the Court Deputy will assign numbers and circulate in due course, with the consultation of Legal Officers of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then, please, have 65 ter 14683 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, General, before I take my chair, could I refer you, in that regard, to paragraph 97 of your statement. There, you referenced a report from General Milovanovic, dated 20 April 1994, to the president of the Republika Srpska, the chief of staff of the Yugoslav Army, as well as corps commands. After reading the first page, I'd like to take you to page 5 of the translation. Have you scanned the first page, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I invite you to now have a look at page 5 of the translation, and direct you, eventually, to the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I see the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, I note, from the date on this document, it immediately precedes the 23 April 1994 agreement you referred to in paragraph 99 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you infer anything from this document, given its date and the context, as to Dr. Karadzic's effective control over forces operating in the Gorazde area at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, I see that the Bosnian Serb Army were responding to the directions of Dr. Karadzic, following the agreement made with Mr. Akashi in Belgrade, or more or less, because, of course, they cheated. They dressed their soldiers as civilians or policemen, and we had a debate about that before they finally withdrew them. In general terms, they conformed with the agreement, finally.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could ask that that eventually be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, this is a duplicate of 65 ter 7650, and it will be Exhibit P1647.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for spotting that duplicate. Your Honour, that does conclude my examination-in-chief now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Now, Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to cross-examine the general. Before the break, we'll have about 10 minutes. So if it is convenient, we can take the break now. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be fine, if it suits you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break for 25 minutes, resuming at 5.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General, Sir Michael. First of all, I would like to thank you for having met up with the Defence. I hope that that will make it possible for us to deal with a great many questions on a yes-or-no basis, so that we spend as little time as possible. As you know, I had asked for 30 hours for this cross-examination. Before we start, in relation to the matters that we agreed upon during this interview that you kindly made possible, I would like to put two or three questions to you in relation to something that truly astonished me. In actual fact, you told me that some people believed that you were of a pro-Serb orientation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That there were even some books that were written along those lines; right? Is this an impartial writer or is it a Muslim lobbyist that wrote that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, you would have to take your own interpretation. Certainly, the books were not balanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what worries me, Sir Michael. Do you agree that very often our relations were chilled, and at certain points in time they were severed altogether?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would say that our relations were imbued with deep personal respect, but, professionally speaking, they were very sharp and we did not consider you to be pro-Serb in the slightest bit; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'm delighted to hear that, because as a United Nations mediator, our job was to remain impartial in our dealings with the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, after this expression of delight of yours, I have to disappoint you. We considered you, perhaps not you, personally, to a certain extent, but the units under your control, we considered you as slightly partial or heavily partial in favour of the Muslim side. You will see, on the basis of our documents, that you were not cautioning them with regard to even major violations, and, on the other hand, you reprimanded the Serbs for much less. Do you agree that we had reason to believe that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There came a moment in the conflict when the United Nations Protection Force became seen by the Bosnian Serb side as less than impartial towards the Serbs, and the reason for that is because NATO failed to fulfill its own obligations with regard to the demilitarisation of Mount Igman, and inevitably the United Nations, who were being supported by NATO, were seen to be party to that failure to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me that you did have some understanding for the few reasons that I mentioned for the dissatisfaction of the Serbs with the UN. So, first of all, it was the sanctions imposed; secondly, Muslim provocations. They were not cautioned about that, but we were cautioned with regard to our response. Thirdly, the partiality of the media; and, fourthly, partiality of a large part of the international community that was biased against the Serbs. Fifth, unfair peace plans that were designed in such a way so that we would refuse them and therefore be exposed to pressures. Sixth, a partial approach to cease-fires, where it was difficult for the Muslims, where they were the losing side, they would ask for a cease-fire, and the entire international community would help them, whereas, where it was hard for us, no one was helping us and nobody asked for a cease-fire. Remember that yesterday I presented these six reasons, as a minimum, and that you said that this may sound convincing from a Serbian perception, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that UNPROFOR did not have any intelligence gathering or any precise information as to the deployment of the warring parties. That was particularly important for us. In Sarajevo, they did not have a full picture as to who was where; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agreed that you did not have full knowledge about the strength and structure of armaments of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was in Sarajevo and around it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, even in your time in 1994, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not an organised military force.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to reply because, as you say, we didn't have any observation of their military capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, we agreed -- or, rather, we established that you did not know that Serbs also lived in Sarajevo during the war. You were especially not aware of the fact that there were between 50.000 and 70.000 of them at the time, right? I mean in the part of Sarajevo that was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I was certainly aware there were Serbs living in Sarajevo during the conflict. Indeed, one of the Bosnian Muslim generals was, in fact, a Serb. But certainly I did not have knowledge that there were 50.000 or 70.000 of them living in Sarajevo at the time. I find that a difficult figure to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Serb general whom you mentioned is Divjak; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also presented a rather accurate approximation of the length of the front-line within Sarajevo between the two warring parties. You said around 70 kilometres. We confirmed that in 1992, it was 42 kilometres, and in 1994, it was 64 kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: In 1994, we thought it was about 70 kilometres, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that the front-line facing Central and Southern Bosnia, that is to say, the external line of separation, was three times longer. It was up to 240 kilometres, approximately; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Your knowledge of that would be better than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that it was at least three times longer than the internal line of separation; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That figure would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that keeping a large number of enemy troops in a small area does have a certain military logic, that it is justified, from a military point of view, to try to keep as many enemy soldiers as possible within a small area; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the point of that remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what you said was that it was only natural that they had three times more soldiers in Sarajevo because that's what they needed from the point of view of their defence. Since they wanted to have a breakthrough, they needed more soldiers than the Serbs did, and, therefore, there were more troops in the central part of Sarajevo. When I asked whether that was justified, from a military point of view, to block and keep enemy troops in a small area, you said that, yes, that would be military logic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think I said that it would be military logic because fighting in a built-up area, which, of course, Sarajevo was, particularly an area which had been subject to bombardment, takes a large number of troops, from whichever perspective, either the attacking or the defence perspective. And so, inevitably, if the Bosnian government forces wished to defend a 70-kilometre frontage which was largely in built-up areas, it would need a large number of troops. I also made the theoretical point to you that it would take, in any point of a line where they wished to attack out -- I do not believe that they did wish to attack out, but had they wanted to, they would have had to assemble three times the number of troops. That is the normal military algorithm for attack against defence. I actually suggested, because of the advantage of the high ground that the Bosnian Serbs controlled, it might take even more than that. That was the theme that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed that I and the Serb side, as a whole, were strongly in favour of the demilitarisation of Sarajevo and placing it under UN administration. However, the Muslim side was persistently opposed to that; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, you confirmed that the United Nations could not determine, unequivocally and with precision, from where sniper fire had come because there weren't any proper investigations that would have established that beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you criticised, to a considerable degree, the UNMOs, the military observers, that they were useless, and sometimes that was stated by way of a joke, and that some of them had even sold out; that you were not satisfied with them and that they were pretty useless to you. I think that you referred to that in some of your statements or in your book.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think you exaggerate my remark somewhat. My view of the United Nations Military Observers was that they came from a mixed background, militarily speaking, they did not all have the necessary experience to read a battle from the tactical point of view, that many of them lived with the parties to the conflict on whom they were supposed to be observing, and their reports, I suspected, were often unreliable. They also had a direct line of communication direct to New York and, therefore, could be subject to propaganda pressure from any of the warring parties. That was my observation. There were, however, many extremely capable military observers who served honourably during that tragic war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Minutes ago, you confirmed with Mr. Karadzic's assertion that the Serbs were strongly in favour of demilitarisation and put it under control of the UN administration, but earlier on you also referred to the policy of intimidating the civilian population. How can these two observations match together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, they were a single -- in pursuit of a single strategy, which was to engineer the demilitarisation of Sarajevo in a way which would allow the lines of conflict to become fixed. This was something, of course -- and it would also -- second point: It would also undermine somewhat the sovereignty of the Bosnian government. Of course, it is the sovereign right of a state to maintain troops on its own territory, particularly in their own capital city. And it was an aim of the Bosnian Serb side to demilitarise the safe areas, which seems a reasonable thing to have suggested, and, of course, it was not accepted by either the Bosnian government or the international community at large, and probably rightly so, although at the time it would have been, in short term, a step towards pacifying the area. And, of course, the demilitarisation of that enclave would have meant the safe -- better safe-guarding of the civil community living there, because no longer would they be caught up in fighting between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that tomorrow we will be able to demonstrate and show documents to prove that we had always been in favour of not accepting the fait accompli and that all the territorial issues would be dealt with by way of a conference. However, you were not in a position to know that because you only came later. Did we agree that the Igman crisis was caused by the fact that the international community and NATO forced us to cede the territory that we had taken on Mount Igman, to return it, actually, and we did return it to the United Nations; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: You're talking about 1993, a time before I arrived. But that was my understanding, when I was briefed on my arrival, and that was the reason for the NATO -- or the withdrawal of the Bosnian Serb forces was the reason for the NATO ultimatum to demilitarise Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to the details thereof later. However, yesterday we agreed on some things, and one of them was that the international community had forced us to return Mount Igman because our stay on Mount Igman would have meant the complete encirclement of Sarajevo. And if we were not on Mount Igman, Sarajevo was not completely encircled; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Two points. First of all, it was my understanding that that was -- to prevent the encirclement of Sarajevo was a reason for the NATO ultimatum to withdraw Serb troops from Sarajevo, and, therefore - your second point - I would agree that it was to allow a line of communication into Sarajevo that was not controlled by the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, I noted in your book, and you confirmed that for me, that Mr. Izetbegovic had often given up on some of the things that had been agreed and went back to square 1, and I am trying to quote you. That's what you said, "square 1"; right? After long negotiations, Mr. Izetbegovic was prone to going back to square 1; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: All parties to the conflict would tend to do that. It was not exclusive to Mr. Izetbegovic. I think you're referring to the going back on the agreement to withdraw heavy weapons and stop firing and bombarding into Sarajevo, and the decision by the Bosnian government side to return Sarajevo to conflict is certainly a point which Mr. Izetbegovic had agreed and went back on. But the general point you make is something which all sides tended to do, depending on their own view of how the conflict was developing and what their own strategic interests were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I had in mind the continuity of such a conduct. For example, we accepted Cutileiro's plan, and then Izetbegovic gave up on it. However, you were familiar with some Serb parts of Sarajevo, for example, Grbavica, and I hope that you could see for yourself that the humanitarian situation there was very difficult. I'm sure that you also saw the traces of shelling as well as the traces of sniping. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The United Nations does not differentiate, when it comes to delivery of humanitarian aid, between the civil populations who may be caught up in the fighting. So the delivery of aid happens to all civilian populations, not just the ones who may be deemed the victims by the international community. Humanitarian aid cannot be seen or used as a weapon in any conflict. So although 2.7 million people were being supported through humanitarian aid, of that number 600.000 were, indeed, Serbs, many of whom lived in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There came a time when you concluded that the situation in Grbavica was even more difficult than in the Muslim part of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There certainly came a time during the summer of 1994 when the aid convoys were flowing into the Bosnian government parts of Sarajevo freely, whereas the Grbavica side was not being supported by those convoys because of the long routes which had to come in through Belgrade, and the establishment of a sanction regime against Belgrade, particularly from the point of fuel, prevented that happening. So certainly at a point in the summer, the Serbs living on the Grbavica side of Sarajevo were in less good condition than the people living on the Bosnian government side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact that after the arrival of humanitarian convoys, the Muslim Army fought even more fiercely, is something that you interpreted in a different way than me. You said it was due to the humanitarian aid, and my interpretation was that it was due to the delivery of ammunition and weapons. But then you presented a very unusual fact, that the first level of humanitarian aid goes to fighters, the second level to the government people, and the third goes to the civilian population. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is a general experience of the delivery of humanitarian aid in conflict. I was not making the specific point about Bosnia. I was saying that is the price that has to be paid for the delivery of humanitarian aid, no matter where in the world that conflict may be taking place. Certainly, it was true of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was Ms. Edgerton who raised the issue of the dubious nature of humanitarian convoys, and we will present a number of documents to show why the Serbs criticised them. Yesterday, I accepted your suggestion that even if there had been any smuggling of fuel and ammunition, that the higher commands of UNPROFOR did not have anything to do with that, and I can agree with that. I accept to live with that. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'm glad you made that point, because I was about to make an intervention with the President, saying that I spotted on the screen that I had not refuted the allegation that the United Nations humanitarian aid convoys were a source of arms or equipment for the Bosnian government forces. Of course, I refute that absolutely, and I'm glad you agreed with me in your last intervention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, yesterday we agreed that that may have been the case, but that your higher commands knew nothing of that. We exculpated your higher commands, but we agreed that things like that may have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It is certainly the case that evidence started to appear on the ground in Bosnia - for example, the provision of new American-style uniforms to the Bosnian forces - that there was some support being given to the federation troops, as they had by then become, and that you will note that the British government, on occasion, raised this issue with the United Nations in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that part, to the issue of territory. However, we agree that yourself could see for yourself that we had been prepared to reduce the territory from 70 per cent to some 50 per cent. Let me ask you this, General: Do you know that the 70 per cent of the territory that we formerly had had a majority Serbian population, that that territory had not been taken by us from the Muslims; that we only wanted to protect our own territory?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't know that, no, and nor would I accept it, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. There's statistical data to that effect. However, can we agree that you criticised the international media that they didn't help and that they were biased and in favour of the Muslim side? Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The media in any conflict, and this is true of Bosnia, are a very good force, particularly when it comes to exposing injustice, human atrocities, suffering, or the breaking of international humanitarian law wherever it may occur, and they are very often -- and they are very good at mobilising the support of the international community to bring about some support to the people who are suffering in these conditions. And the media in Sarajevo was no -- in the Bosnian war was no different. However, inevitably, over a period of time the media started to take moral positions about what they thought should be done to regress the aggressions which they perceived had taken place. And by the time I arrived in Bosnia, there was no doubt about it, that there was a major media initiative to try and mobilise the West to back the deployment of NATO into Bosnia and withdraw the United Nations peacekeeping forces. It was a general theme running throughout 1994 that that was what the duty -- a moral duty, indeed, of the international community should be. I felt that was wrong for 1994, but I strongly believe that's what should have happened at the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about the Bosnian government, Sir Michael, and when you're talking about the aggression, you were there long enough in order to be aware of the essence of our relations. Do you agree that we Bosnian Serbs are from Bosnia, that we had not come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: As I said, Dr. Karadzic, we had no knowledge of the make-up of the parties -- the forces belonging to the parties to the conflict on any of the sides. So where the forces came from, how many they were, how they were equipped, et cetera, was -- our knowledge was haphazard, not systematic, and so it would be impossible to make any sort of comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you briefed about the fact that the Serbs made up one-third of the state government, and that one-third of the state monopoly was in the hands of the Serbs, and that Professors Koljevic and Plavsic were on an equal footing in that Presidency with Mr. Izetbegovic? And I'm talking about the time before the Presidency broke up.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, I focused on what my prime task was, which was the delivery of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, and you were very successful in that. However, with all due respect, allow me to say that when one refers to the government, on the one hand, you're suggesting that the rebels are on the other side. Your [as interpreted] thesis is that the state monopoly of a force and the state organism broke up and was divided into three different pieces, three constituent people. Were you not supposed to be told that the Serbs were not rebels, but, rather, one-third of the legitimate government, of the legitimate power in that state? In the transcript, it should read "our thesis," not "your thesis," because it is the Serbian thesis. Wouldn't it be appropriate for somebody to have briefed you and told you that the Serbs were not rebels but part of that state, part of the government, part of the state organism, so as to help you know who you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The Bosnian government and the Bosnian nation were a state recognised by the United Nations. No reference was made at that time to the so-called Republika Srpska, and quite rightly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. It won't be difficult to prove that on a different occasion. Did we also agree that you responded to General Mladic's question and invitation and that you took the responsibility for NATO strikes in the sector of Gorazde, when NATO was invited to engage in air-strikes in the area of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: After due warning to withdraw the armour and artillery that was attacking Gorazde by the -- attacks being made by the Bosnian Serb forces, after due warning, when the attacks continued, air-strikes were called against those artillery positions and against that armour. And, indeed, it was I who was part of that process of calling for air-strikes. My mission under United Nations Security Council 824 [Realtime transcript read in error "834"] and 836, was to use all means possible to deter attacks against those enclaves, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we agree that the attacks were called not because of the fact that your forces had come under attack, but rather because Gorazde, as an enclave, had come under attack?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I point out a correction on the previous paragraph? That is, my statement should have read "under Security Council Resolutions 824 and 836."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer your question, Dr. Karadzic: The air-strikes were called because of the Bosnian Serb forces' attack into the enclave of Gorazde. The fact that there were United Nations personnel in that enclave was coincidental. The attacks would have been called whether they were there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, General, sir, since we have dealt with the position of your pro-Serbian position, and the air-strikes fall under that, can I then count on your knightly and army honour that the pro-Serbian influences will not -- or pro-Serbian bias will not influence your answers and that your answers will not be pro-Serbian, either consciously or subconsciously, during this cross-examination? In other words, can you still be objective, although there was an impression that at one point in time you were of pro-Serbian orientation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the point. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to make sure that some questions will not be anti-Serbian in order to allow Sir Michael to prove that he's not pro-Serbian, although we have already managed to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in your book, "Fighting For Peace: A Lesson From Bosnia," on page 25, which is page 35 in e-court, you describe the welcome that was provided to you by Muslim soldiers when you first arrived in Sarajevo, and your associate, Mr. Andreev, explained to you that that was customary. Whenever a guest or a high official arrived, Muslims opened fire on Serbs in order to provoke a response and to portray themselves as a victim, and you say that Andreev told you this: [In English] "... that civilians mattered less to the Bosnian government than images of suffering and war."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so. I mean, what I'm -- the point I'm making is not necessarily that that was a true statement by Victor Andreev, but that is what he told me on my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he say that to you on the basis of his previous experience with other people? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: He would have to speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, on page 35 in e-court, in this same book, you said, I will quote: [In English] "The indecency had been banished --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we have that as well? What is the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1037, Sir Michael's book. It's a voluminous book. We don't have enough time to deal with it in its entirety, so we'll just be dealing with brief excerpts: [In English] "The indecency had been banished to another world in which the ends always justified the means. Obviously, my first task would be to tell President Izetbegovic that this grim strategy of inflicting such horrors on his own people would never succeed, and that I would do all in my power to prevent the UN from becoming engaged in a war in Bosnia as a combatant."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'm just looking in the pages that you referred to. You said "page 35." Not in my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 18 in the book.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: 18 in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's 18 in the book, but it's 35 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: You must be referring to the hard-copy version, because it's not in my paperback version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, page 18 in the book, and it's page 35 in e-court. But it seems to be a different edition. We seem to have a different edition from you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That's okay, I can read it on the screen. So which paragraph are you referring to, Dr. Karadzic, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In "Fighting For Peace," it is page 18, or, rather, 064 is the ERN number, 107-997. It's the one-but-last paragraph, and then it says: [In English] "... in New York, this tactic of the Bosnian government to Madeleine Albright. She confirmed that the US Administration knew what was happening, but could do little about it. Now the quiet, civilised apartment overlooking the East River, where we had discussions, Bosnia seemed very far from the shattered city and the noisy bombardment I was witnessing. Here, humanity and decency ..." Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I found it on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That's what I wrote, and I that's what I no doubt said to Madeleine Albright at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Further on, you confirmed, in your testimony in General Galic's trial on page 10210 -- during the examination-in-chief, you said that there was evidence to the effect that there were suspicions that the Bosnian government was intentionally targeting civilians within the lines of conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'll just wait for it to come on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I paraphrased it, actually, but I can quote it now, if you wish. Do you remember that statement? Judge Orie asked you -- asked you -- 10210, that's the page reference. Judge Orie asked you -- [In English] Asked you -- wait until the cursor stops moving. {Interpretation] This was an objection, wasn't it? [In English] "There was certainly some suspicion, before I arrived in Sarajevo, that allegations had appeared in the media, and there was certainly suspicion that that was happening after I arrived. What was certain was that the Bosnian government forces would, from time to time, fire at the Serbs at a particular moment of political importance in order to draw back fire on Sarajevo so that the Bosnian government could demonstrate the continuing plight of the people in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: And your point, Dr. Karadzic, is: Is that what I said during the hearing or is that something which you believe I should confirm or deny now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just confirm whether that's what you said in the proceedings against General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, without having the original document in front of me, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll put a question. Actually, the one that was put to you there: [In English] "So now, on the other side of the coin, so as to speak, during the time that you were in Sarajevo, were there any incidents that came to your attention, in terms of reports, investigations conducted by the UN, which suggested that forces on the side of the confrontation lines controlled by Bosnian government forces had deliberately targeted civilians within the confrontation lines?" Your answer was: "There was certainly some suspicions, but before I arrived." I can give you this, if you --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, that is correct, there were definitely rumours to that effect, in the United Nations forces, that the Bosnian government forces had been firing on their own civilians in order to create the images of suffering and maintain the feeling that the international community should come to the help of the Bosnian state, in military terms, rather than just delivering humanitarian aid. That was certainly something which was currently thought may be a possibility at the time, but it was -- I think no evidence could ever be found to prove that suspicion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then call up in e-court 1D2257.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were still there. It's the 9th of November. Perhaps you were away at the moment, but you were still commander there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document. The date is the 9th of November. The Bosnian police was present -- actually presented a report to a judge, Mr. Krsnatovic [phoen], Livanjska Ulica, shelling, two 82-millimetre mortar shells. We can all see that. Now let's move on to page 2, the angle of descent. The estimate is between 70 and 75 degrees. And then page 3, "Conclusion": [In English] "It is possible to conclude that the most suspected area are under the control of B and H. To fire from the BSA positions with the same range and with the same angle of descent, direction of the mortar should be 4.200 milliems from Grdonj," although Grdonj was under Muslim control. [Interpretation] Last sentence: [In English] "The BSA positions and from the same direction between 1.200 and 1.600 milliems, the distance should be at least 3.700 metres. The angle of descent in that case would be less than 60 degrees." [Interpretation] So here are some findings, and this was actually handed over to a judge in Sarajevo, stating that they had shelled Livanjska Street themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That's what the report appears to say, certainly. However, I have to warn that the identification of the firing point of a mortar is -- from looking at the shell scrapes, I discovered it was a very inexact science and that a number of cases -- I can certainly thing of one where a different view had to be taken as a result of other information or better investigation as to what had happened. The UN had deployed some mortar-tracking radars, but they were fairly primitive, given today's capability, and weren't able to cover the whole city. So although this report seems conclusive, I would warn that it may not be as conclusive as you seem to think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir Michael, you are saying that in general terms. You're saying that this method is not a very reliable one, generally speaking, on the whole; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is, more or less, so. Looking at the -- depending on the number of shells and the angle of -- and I'm not a technician here -- the angle of attack, the more steep the angle, the more difficult it is to determine the distance and the direction. That is so. I mean, one shell is more difficult than four shells, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this document with the 65 ter number 1D2257 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in General Galic's transcript, on page 012011, you said, during your examination-in-chief -- or, rather, you established that -- actually, what we read out a few moments ago, from that same document -- I mean, from your book, that is; namely, that the Muslim forces -- you called them the Bosnian government, but we're the Bosnian government too. So the Muslim forces were firing at the Serbs, with the objective of attracting their fire; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't mean to say they were firing. I was saying there was a suspicion when I arrived that that may have been the case on occasions, but there was no firm evidence ever presented to me that that was something that the Bosnian government was doing as a matter of policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you have your statement, amalgamated statement, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's coming to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got the one of the 13th of January, but not the opening statement which Ms. Edgerton read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got that one, yes, the big one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have the paragraph 215 there, under the subheading "The BH Army alleged responsibility for attacking Sarajevo," you said that, I quote: "I am certain, however, that Bosnian government forces would, from time to time, fire at Serbs at particular moments in order to draw backfire onto Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that was often done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, we have all these in evidence already. You don't have to go into detail one by one again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm afraid that the book is too important, as a whole. It is a piece of literature, after all. And yesterday we agreed that General Rose wrote that with a bit of poetic license, so we, as the Defence, have to spell certain things out in very specific terms so that they would be de-literalised, as it were. It is wonderful to read this book, because it is beautifully written from a literary point of view, but in matters of criminal law we have to see what facts are, on the one hand, and what feelings and opinions are, on the other. Also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a question for the party. What's the status of Sir Michael's book? It's in our evidence. I noted it's exhibited as D162, but my recollection is only one page was -- only a couple of pages were admitted. I should correct -- I should stand corrected if I'm wrong. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We were just discussing that with my colleague. I think that's exactly the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, can I just make the intervention, in reply to Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that there is no poetic license in that book. Whatever its literary merits may or may not be, it was written, and I explained to the counsel for Dr. Karadzic yesterday, it was written from a close scrutiny of the UN records which I had at the time, and newspaper cuttings and other sources, including some notes I had taken myself, which, sadly, got destroyed on the computer subsequently. But there is no poetic license in that book at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am waiting for the interpretation to be finished. I'm waiting for the interpretation. And this is what this is all about: We have an amalgamated statement by General Rose. However, the whole book has not been admitted, and nor would I like it to be admitted until it is de-literalised or de-poetised before we can establish what facts indeed are in the book. And also we do not have his testimony in the International Criminal Court, we don't have his -- in the ICJ, rather, and we don't have all the other statements and testimonies by General Rose before this Tribunal; for example, in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the time for you to put questions to the witness. Don't make statements. It's not helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just explaining why I tend to go over the same ground every now and then. I'm forced to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in the Galic case, on page 10211, you said that the Bosnian Muslim forces, according to your opinion, had had three tanks and some heavy artillery that they hid in the tunnel. Yesterday, we agreed that the tunnel was very close to your base. And in the transcript, you go on to say this: [In English] "... out from time to time, particularly after the cease-fire in September, and fire at the Bosnian Serbs in order to attract fire back." [Interpretation] And then you also said that you protested with the Bosnian Muslim government with regard to such incidents, and that you raised those protests all the time, and that those protests: [In English] "... were mainly to Mr. Ganic, who seemed to head up the military operations on the Bosnian government side." [Interpretation] Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement dated 24 May 1995, on page 4 - the ER number is 104-4294 - you also stated that two Swedish APCs were destroyed at Tribnica [phoen]. Close-air support was agreed with NATO, and flights were made overhead. However, the attacks were stopped without engaging the Bosnian Serb forces. You spoke to Generals Mladic and Milovanovic, and you warned them that such attacks would be met with appropriate force. Their response was that they had been responding to a BiH attack, and they then accused the BiH of attacking the Swedes. And further on, you notice: [In English] "... advise them if we have any moment in sensitive areas so that there should be no repeat of this incident. This includes -- indicated that the Bosnian Serb Army had been responsible." [Interpretation] Do you agree that it was necessary for the Republika Srpska Army to know where your vehicles were at all times, where any of your vehicles were?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Sorry, which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Galic transcript, page 10211, and this is about a Swedish APC which had been destroyed by the Serbs without the Serbs even being aware of its presence, because there had been an exchange of fire with the Muslim Army, and that's how it transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, I was rising to be of assistance. That's paragraph 53 in General Rose's amalgamated statement of January 2009. And Dr. Karadzic's question is -- I object to that. It's an absolutely unwarranted statement. Lines 20 to 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, now are you able to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember the incident when the two APCs were destroyed, and I remember making a warning to the Bosnian Serbs side that we would take appropriate action if it happened again. And we would have done so had we been, at the time, able to identify the Bosnian Serb Army positions from where the fire had come. That's what I remember about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in general terms, and also with regard to this situation and the passage of certain units or smaller UNPROFOR groups, do you remember that the Serbian side asked to be informed about those movements; that only if the Serbian Army knew about those movements they could be held responsible of anything that might occur?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We always warned the Bosnian Serb side of any movements of UNPROFOR forces or, indeed, convoys, aid convoys, through their controlled territory. We never moved without prior warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, tomorrow we will show you that there were such cases and that the incidents were created because the Serbian Army was not aware of the presence of your smaller groups and forces. General, do you remember, in the Gorazde crisis and the communication between you and Akashi, who was with me and Mladic, when we finally established that the Muslim Army had brought your men to a position where nobody expected them, and when the Muslims withdrew, they remained exposed to the Serbian Army threats? Do you remember that incident? Some other people described the same situation in some other texts.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: You're referring to the deployment of the Joint Commission officers in the Gorazde enclave. They were not directed by the Bosnian forces to take up their positions. They chose those positions, themselves, because that's where they felt they could get the best visibility as to what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you remember that there was a misunderstanding and that the misunderstanding originated from the fact that they found themselves in wrong coordinates, where nobody expected them, right, and that they did not withdraw simultaneously with the Muslim units, and that they thus remained encircled or semi-encircled by the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is more or less the situation that happened, but, of course, it was -- you should not forget that the coordinates that we gave you before the JCOs were deployed were all heavily shelled by the Bosnian Serb artillery shortly after the air-strikes. Fortunately, the JCOs had moved from these positions to the ones where they were when the air-strikes occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, sir, I believe you describe that event in your book. Mr. Akashi and I were in Pale together with Mr. Stoltenberg and Churkin. Mladic was in the field, and you were somewhere else, and finally we established that your monitors or, rather, the forward air controllers, or whoever, were in the Muslim combat deployment area, in the Muslim trenches, where the Serbs did not expect it. What I'm trying to do is to use that example in order to see whether there was an intent to harm UN soldiers or vehicles or, rather, were those just misunderstandings that originated from a poor communication about the positions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: They were never in Bosnian Army trenches. They were on a bend in the road when they were hit by Serb fire, and it was accepted at the time by both the JCOs and by my own command that this had not been a deliberate attack by the Bosnian Serbs; they had been caught between the cross-fires of the two opposing sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your book, "Fighting For Peace" - in e-court, it is on page 26, and it is possible that this is part of the introduction to your book - in any case, you wrote that the Bosnian Government, and I quote: [In English] "... original aim of getting the US and NATO committed to the war on the ground." [Interpretation] They tried to receive the support of the media circus, as you called it, in Sarajevo by promoting the images of war and suffering, and the Bosnian Government was thus in a position to appeal directly to the international community to do something, and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A favour, please, Your Honour, from Dr. Karadzic. If I could ask he actually quotes the page number of the hard-copy book that he's referring to, it would certainly help me, in any case, find the page reference, especially until we have the book electronically available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, when you are planning to refer to a certain part of a document, let them have it before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if it's still in e-court. If it were, then it would be 26. And in the book, it's page 9. At least, in our edition of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the English booth does not have the original of the book in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's now on the monitor, page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your opinion and your conclusion with regard to the manoeuvres of the Muslim side or, rather, their attempts to manipulate the international opinion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: My words, as written, are what I thought then, when I wrote them, and what I think now to be the case. I did not use the word "manipulation," I don't think, in my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I used the word, but it does look like a manipulation to me. And we knew and we agreed that attempts were made for the whole world to be turned against us. Can we look at the following sentence: [In English] "UN peacekeeping efforts to halt the fighting were clearly an obstacle to their endeavours, and by 1994 it became obvious to us in Sarajevo that the UN's primary concern to alleviate the suffering of the people was of less consequence to Bosnia's leaders than the achievement of their own political goals." [Interpretation] Right? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so. That was my view, and still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were quite unhappy with the positions of Mr. Ganic on various occasions, and here, for example, in your book "Fighting For Peace" - in e-court, 187 - you speak about fire being opened on a UN aircraft. He knew that it had been sent from the Bosnian side, and on one occasion a French soldier was seen as having been shot at from the Bosnian side, from Butmir, across the airport. A mortar fire was -- a machine-gun fire was opened on that French soldier while the aircraft was being loaded. The Bosnian side obviously did that in order to preserve the image of a city under siege. And Ganic agreed that such attacks should be stopped, but he never followed through. And you say: [In English] "He was even less co-operative when it came to stopping the fighting in Bihac." [Interpretation] Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly, I remember the incident, as described in my book, when the mortar fire came from across the airfield towards the terminal buildings which, of course, the French were located in. And I also remember raising the matter with Mr. Ganic. The machine-gun fire, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time to adjourn for the day, so we'll resume tomorrow in the afternoon again at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
